lessons.title: Knowing when grapes are ripe
lessons.html:
Knowing when grapes are ripe

Grapes do not ripen any more after they are picked. If they are picked too early, they are sour. If they are picked too late, they lose quality, rot, or are eaten by birds. So the right picking day is very important. In the Western Cape most wine grapes are harvested from about January to March.

Who decides?

The farm manager and the winemaker or buyer decide when each block is picked. They check:

  • Sugar: measured with a refractometer in degrees Balling. Each wine style needs a certain sugar level.
  • Acid: grapes lose acid as they ripen; the cellar tests this.
  • Taste and seeds: ripe grapes taste sweet and fruity; seeds turn brown.
  • Health: if rot is starting, picking may be brought forward.
  • Weather: rain forecast may change the plan.

For table grapes, the buyer's standards also set the colour, berry size and sugar needed for export.

Taking a grape sample

You may be asked to collect samples. Walk through the block in a zig-zag and pick berries from many vines: from both sides of the row, from the top and bottom of bunches, and from bunches in the sun and in the shade. Put them in a labelled bag with the block name and date. A sample from only one or two vines does not show the true ripeness.

Getting ready

  • Clean picking crates or lugs and clean bins.
  • Sharp picking scissors or knives.
  • Gloves, hat, closed shoes, water bottle.
  • The picking plan: which block, which rows, how many bins.

Pickers must wash their hands before work and after using the toilet. Grapes are food.

lessons.title: Picking and handling the grapes
lessons.html:
Picking and handling the grapes

How to pick

  1. Hold the bunch gently by the stalk, not by the berries.
  2. Cut the stalk with scissors close to the shoot. Do not pull or twist the bunch off the vine.
  3. Place the bunch gently in the crate. Do not throw it.
  4. Remove leaves, rotten or sunburnt berries and any rubbish, as instructed.
  5. Do not overfill crates. Grapes squashed at the bottom lose juice and start to spoil.
  6. Pick all the ripe bunches on the vine, including hidden ones inside the canopy and low down.

What must NOT go into the crate

  • Leaves, canes and wire.
  • Rotten, mouldy or diseased bunches (unless told otherwise).
  • Stones, soil and plastic.
  • Bunches from a different block or cultivar.

Table grapes

Table grapes are handled even more gently. Hold the stalk, not the berries, so the natural white bloom stays on. Pack them as the pack house standard says. Damaged bunches will be rejected.

Keep grapes cool and moving

  • Many farms pick early in the morning, when it is cool.
  • Keep full crates in the shade until they are collected.
  • Get grapes to the cellar or pack house quickly.

Safety

  • Keep scissors pointing down when walking; keep fingers away from the blade.
  • Lift crates with bent knees; carry them close to your body. Do not stack them too high.
  • Stay clear of tractors and trailers. Make sure the driver sees you.
  • Watch out for bees and wasps at harvest time. If you are allergic, tell your supervisor before work.
  • Do not enter a block that has been sprayed until the supervisor confirms it is safe.
  • Drink water often.

Records

Supervisors record the block, date, number of crates or bins, and each picker's count if the farm pays per crate.

Key points

  • Grapes do not ripen after picking; the manager and cellar choose the picking day.
  • Sample berries from many vines in a zig-zag.
  • Cut, do not pull; hold the stalk and place bunches gently.
  • Keep leaves, rot, stones and other blocks' grapes out of the crate.
  • Keep grapes cool, work safely and wash hands.
